'''James Arthur Jackson''' (born October 14, 1970) is an American former professional [[basketball]] player. Over his 14 [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) seasons, Jackson was on the active roster of 12 different teams, which was an NBA record shared with [[Joe Smith (basketball)|Joe Smith]], [[Tony Massenburg]], [[Chucky Brown]], and [[Ish Smith]]; until Ish played with the [[Denver Nuggets]], his 13th team, in the [[2022-23 NBA season|2022–23 season]].<ref>BasketballReference.com{{cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/leaders/most_franchises.html|title=Most Teams}}</ref> He is currently a basketball analyst for [[Fox Sports (United States)|Fox Sports]], [[Turner Sports]] and the [[Los Angeles Clippers]] on [[Bally Sports West]], having previously worked for the [[Big Ten Network]]. Jim Jackson also works as an analyst for the NBA Playoffs on NBATV.

He was a key member of the French junior national team and played at the [[INSEP]]. In 2004, he won the [[Ligue Nationale de Basketball|French League]] title with [[ÉB Pau-Orthez|Pau-Orthez]]. Petro has also represented the [[French national basketball team]].

'''Jeryl Henry Braxton Sasser Jr.''' (born February 13, 1979) is an American former professional [[basketball]] player.<ref name=bio>{{Cite web|url=http://virtussports.com/Clients/bios%5CJeryl%20Sasser%20bio.pdf|title=Jerryl Sasser bio|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717213442/http://virtussports.com/Clients/bios%5CJeryl%20Sasser%20bio.pdf |archive-date=2011-07-17 }}</ref> Sasser played [[college basketball]] for the [[SMU Mustangs men's basketball|SMU Mustangs]] and professionally in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) for the [[Orlando Magic]].

Born in [[Dallas, Texas]], Sasser graduated from [[Justin F. Kimball High School]] and played [[college basketball]] at [[Southern Methodist University]] (SMU).  He was selected by the [[Orlando Magic]] as the 22nd overall pick in the [[2001 NBA draft]].

In two seasons for the Magic (his only time in the NBA) he averaged 2.5 points and 2.3 rebounds per game. Sasser's final NBA game was played in Game 7 of the Eastern Conference First Round on May 4, 2003. In that game, Orlando would drop the series to the Detroit Pistons, losing Game 7 93-108, with Sasser recording 3 points and 1 rebound.

He also played with the [[Yakima Sun Kings]] of the [[Continental Basketball Association]], and with [[France|French]] [[Ligue Nationale de Basketball#Pro A|Pro A]] team [[Élan Béarnais Pau-Orthez]]. In November 2005, Sasser signed for [[Bnei HaSharon]] in [[Israel]] replacing injured [[Cookie Belcher]],<ref name=safsal>{{Cite web|url=http://www.safsal.co.il/earticle.aspx?id=4308|title=Sasser to Replace Belcher|access-date=August 22, 2007|archive-date=October 8, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071008050054/http://www.safsal.co.il/earticle.aspx?id=4308|url-status=dead}}</ref> but he was released after two games. From 2007 to 2009, he played for Al Arabi in Kuwait, and was a Kuwait League Champion in 2008.<ref name=bio/>

Jeryl Sasser is the younger brother of former NBA player [[Jason Sasser]].<ref name=safsal/>


'''Post-playing Career'''

After retiring from professional basketball, Sasser became involved in religious teaching. As of 2025, he serves as a teacher and elder with [[Yah’s Hidden Ones]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://yahshiddenones.com/}}</ref> a religious congregation based in Irving, Texas.

'''Jimmy'''<!--Do not put James as his first name and Jimmy as a nickname, as the latter is already his first name.--> '''Butler III''' (born September 14, 1989) is an American professional [[basketball]] player for the [[Golden State Warriors]] of the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA). Nicknamed "'''Jimmy Buckets'''", he is a six-time [[NBA All-Star]], a five-time [[All-NBA Team]] member, and a five-time [[NBA All-Defensive Team]] member.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Urbina |first1=Frank |title=20 greatest small forwards ever: The HoopsHype list |url=https://www.hoopshype.com/story/sports/nba/2025/07/28/20-greatest-small-forwards-ever-the-hoopshype-list/85410136007/ |website=HoopsHype |access-date=November 23, 2025 |date=July 28, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=20 greatest defensive small forwards ever: The HoopsHype list |url=https://www.hoopshype.com/story/sports/nba/rankings/2025/02/25/20-greatest-defensive-small-forwards-ever-the-hoopshype-list/79228509007/ |website=HoopsHype |access-date=November 23, 2025 |date=February 25, 2025}}</ref> He won a gold medal as a member of the [[2016 United States men's Olympic basketball team|2016 U.S. Olympic team]].

Butler played one year of [[college basketball]] for [[Tyler Junior College]] before transferring to [[Marquette Golden Eagles men's basketball|Marquette University]]. He was selected with the 30th overall pick in the [[2011 NBA draft]] by the [[Chicago Bulls]]. In 2015, he was named the [[NBA Most Improved Player Award|NBA Most Improved Player]]. After six seasons in Chicago, he was traded to the [[Minnesota Timberwolves]] in June 2017, and was then again traded in November 2018, this time to the [[Philadelphia 76ers]]. In July 2019, he signed with the [[Miami Heat]]. During his first season with the team, Butler reached the [[2020 NBA Finals|NBA Finals]]. In 2021, he led the league in [[steal (basketball)|steals]]. In 2023, Butler and the eighth-seeded Heat played in the [[2023 NBA Finals]], their second appearance in four years.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Thomas |first1=Louisa |title=The Legend of Playoff Jimmy |url=https://www.newyorker.com/sports/sporting-scene/the-legend-of-playoff-jimmy |magazine=The New Yorker |access-date=April 20, 2024 |date=April 13, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Bailey |first1=Andy |title=Ranking the Top 50 NBA Playoff Performers of All Time |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/10124068-ranking-the-top-50-nba-playoff-performers-of-all-time |website=[[Bleacher Report]] |access-date=June 22, 2024 |date=June 18, 2024}}</ref> Amidst conflicts with the Heat's front office, Butler was traded to the Warriors in 2025.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Jimmy Butler era in Miami was special despite rocky ending |url=https://www.nba.com/news/jimmy-butler-makes-miami-return |website=NBA.com |access-date=March 25, 2025 |date=March 25, 2025}}</ref>

'''Jerrelle Benimon''' (born August 1, 1991) is an American former professional [[basketball]] player. In college, he was the 2012–13 [[Colonial Athletic Association Men's Basketball Player of the Year|Colonial Athletic Association Player of the Year]] as a [[redshirt (sports)|redshirt]] junior after leading the [[Towson Tigers men's basketball|Towson Tigers]] to the greatest single-season turnaround in [[National Collegiate Athletic Association]] (NCAA) [[Division I (NCAA)|Division I]] history; the Tigers finished with a 1–31 record in 2011–12 before completing an 18–13 season the following year. Benimon also tied for the second-highest rebounding average (11.2) in Division I behind only [[Siena Saints men's basketball|Siena]]'s [[O. D. Anosike]]'s 11.4 per game average. Benimon repeated as the player of the year as a [[senior (education)|senior]] in 2013–14 and, coincidentally, finished second in the national rebounding average for a second consecutive season (11.2).
